D7: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement

CCAR-P study guide · the smallest domain, tested at the architect level
Weight 7% ≈ 4 of 63 questions 120 min · 720/1000 to pass $175 · Pearson VUE proctored

What this domain is really about

You are the architect who rolls out Claude-powered tools to a whole engineering org and keeps them running. Three jobs: (1) configure tools like Claude Code so 200 developers get the same safe, consistent setup; (2) design AI-assisted workflows that speed developers up without letting bad code ship faster; (3) debug production Claude systems and write the runbooks the on-call team follows at 3am. The exam tests design decisions and trade-offs here, not memorized config flags.

Three official objectives, and this volume covers each one fully:

  1. Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (for example, Claude Code).
  2. Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling.
  3. Support debugging and operational issue resolution.

1. Rolling out Claude Code across an org: configuration layers

What it is. Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: it reads your repo, runs commands, edits files, and calls tools on your behalf. When one developer uses it, configuration is a personal preference. When 200 developers use it, configuration is governance. Configuration layers are the stacked sources of settings, where a higher layer overrides a lower one, so the org can set non-negotiable guardrails while teams and individuals still customize their own workflow.

Why it exists. Without layers you get three failures at once. First, drift: every developer's install behaves differently, so "it worked on my machine" becomes "it worked with my settings." Second, unenforceable policy: if security's rules live in a file any developer can edit, they are suggestions, not controls. Third, painful onboarding: each new hire hand-configures everything instead of inheriting the team's setup from the repo.

Under the hood: the four layers

Settings resolve from the most specific authority down to defaults. From highest to lowest precedence:

  1. Managed (enterprise) policy. Set by IT or platform admins, pushed to every machine (for example, via device management). The developer cannot override this layer. This is where compliance rules live: allowed models, data-handling policy, hard deny rules.
  2. Project settings (.claude/settings.json in the repo). Checked into version control, so everyone who clones the repo inherits the team's setup: shared permissions, shared hooks, project conventions. A personal settings.local.json alongside it holds per-developer tweaks that are gitignored.
  3. User settings (~/.claude/settings.json). Personal defaults that follow the developer across every repo.
  4. Built-in defaults. What the tool does when nobody configured anything.

Context files follow a parallel idea. CLAUDE.md files give the agent persistent instructions, and they exist at four scopes: an enterprise-level file from admins, a project-level file in the repo (team conventions, architecture notes), a user-level file (personal preferences), and a local per-project file (CLAUDE.local.md, gitignored, for personal overrides). The agent loads the applicable ones together, so repo knowledge travels with the repo instead of living in one person's head.

Merge subtlety that the exam loves

For most settings, a more specific layer replaces a less specific one. But permissions merge with deny winning: if project settings deny a destructive command and the user's personal settings allow it, the deny still holds. And nothing in any lower layer can touch managed policy. Two consequences: a developer's local edits cannot weaken org guardrails, and a repo's checked-in settings protect every contributor automatically.

Worked example (illustrative numbers). A 200-engineer fintech rolls out Claude Code. The platform team ships managed policy with 12 deny rules (no rm -rf, no sudo, no pushing to main without review tooling, no network calls to non-allowlisted hosts). Each repo gets a checked-in .claude/settings.json with the team's test commands and a project CLAUDE.md describing the service architecture. Onboarding drops from about 2 hours of manual setup per developer to roughly 15 minutes (install, sign in, clone). When one developer tries to allow sudo npm install in their personal settings to "move faster," the managed deny rule still blocks it, and the attempt is logged.

Common misunderstanding

"Project settings replace user settings, so the repo controls everything." Wrong in two ways. First, permissions merge with deny-first rather than replacing. Second, a developer can edit the repo's settings file locally, so project-level rules are team convention, not org enforcement. Only the managed layer is truly non-overridable. If the scenario mentions compliance, regulators, or "even if a developer changes their own settings," the answer lives in the managed layer.

Exam relevance: D7 asks who controls what during a rollout. Read every scenario for the constraint: compliance or "cannot be overridden" points to managed policy; team consistency points to checked-in project settings; personal preference points to user settings.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A healthcare company rolls out Claude Code to 150 engineers. Compliance requires that no developer can enable a model the security team has not approved, even by editing local files." Select one.

Trap: an answer like "add the approved model list to each repo's .claude/settings.json" looks team-friendly but is locally editable, so it fails the "even by editing local files" constraint. The credited answer pins the model allowlist in managed (enterprise) policy, the only layer a developer cannot override.

2. Permissions and guardrails: allow, ask, deny, plus hooks

What it is. Claude Code is an agent: it takes actions in the real world (running shell commands, editing files, fetching URLs). The permission system decides, for each attempted action, whether it runs silently, pauses for human approval, or is blocked outright. Three outcomes: allow (run without asking), ask (prompt the developer first), deny (block and log).

Why it exists. An agent with no permission model has an unlimited blast radius (the amount of damage one bad action can do). The model might run git push --force on the wrong branch, curl a malicious URL from a compromised dependency's README, or delete a directory it misread. Permissions shrink the blast radius to what the org has explicitly accepted.

Under the hood

Every tool call is pattern-matched against the merged permission rules before it executes. Rules look like Bash(npm run test:*) (allow), Bash(sudo *) (deny), or WebFetch (ask). The first matching rule decides. On conflict between layers, deny wins.

Hooks are the programmatic enforcement point. A hook is a shell command the tool runs automatically at a lifecycle moment: PreToolUse (right before a tool runs, can block or modify it), PostToolUse (after, for logging or validation), Stop (when the agent finishes, for cleanup or checks), and session events like SessionStart. The classic enterprise pattern is a PreToolUse hook that scans every Bash command against a denylist or a secret pattern and blocks it before the model ever sees the result. Because hooks run with the developer's own shell privileges, hook definitions themselves must be managed at the project or managed layer in high-trust environments; a user-editable hook is a hole, not a control.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(git status)", "Read(//repo/src/**)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)", "WebFetch"],
    "deny":  ["Bash(sudo *)", "Bash(rm -rf *)", "Bash(curl *)"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "/opt/guardrails/scan-command.sh"}]}
    ]
  }
}

Reading the example: tests and reads run freely; pushes and web fetches pause for approval; anything with sudo, recursive delete, or curl is hard-blocked. Before every Bash call, scan-command.sh gets the final say and can veto.

Worked example (illustrative). A platform team audits one quarter of agent sessions: about 12% triggered at least one "ask" prompt, and post-rollout surveys showed developers approved 97% of asks within seconds. After that finding, the team moved the genuinely dangerous patterns (destructive git operations, package publishes) from ask to deny at the managed layer. Destructive-command incidents fell to zero the next quarter, and "ask" volume dropped by half because asks were reserved for real judgment calls.

Common misunderstanding

"Ask is a safety control." Ask is a speed bump, not a control. Developers under deadline click through prompts (prompt fatigue), so ask only slows accidents; it does not prevent them. Deny is the only hard control. The exam exploits this: whenever the scenario demands a guarantee ("must never," "compliance requires"), ask is the trap and deny is the answer.

Exam relevance: D7 frames permissions as the blast-radius control for agentic tools. Expect trade-off questions: velocity (allow) versus safety (deny), and where enforcement must live (managed layer) to survive local edits.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "After a rollout, an agent ran git push --force and overwrote a release branch. The team had set push commands to 'ask.' What control would have prevented this?" Select one.

Trap: "require ask for all Bash commands" or "train developers to read prompts carefully." Both keep the human as the safety mechanism, and humans under deadline click through. The credited answer is a deny rule on destructive git patterns at the managed layer, which removes the human from the critical path entirely.

3. Distributing MCP servers to teams

What it is. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that connects Claude to external tools and data through MCP servers: small services that expose tools (for example, "search the docs," "read a ticket," "check CI status"). Distributing MCP servers means deciding which servers every developer gets, who vets them, and whose credentials they use, instead of letting each developer hand-wire their own.

Why it exists. Ad-hoc MCP sprawl is a quiet disaster. One developer adds an unvetted server with write access to the production database; another pastes a personal API key into a config file that gets committed. Nobody can answer "which tools can our agents touch right now," and when a contractor leaves, nobody knows which keys to rotate. Central distribution turns the tool surface into an inventory: known servers, known scopes, one place to revoke.

Under the hood

MCP server configurations live in .mcp.json files at project scope (at the repo root, checked into the repo, shared by the team), and in the user's Claude Code config at local scope (this project only, the default) and user scope (all projects). The org pattern has three parts:

  1. A vetted registry. A central catalog of approved MCP servers. Each entry records what the server can do, what data it touches, and its risk tier. Adding a server is a review decision, like adding a dependency.
  2. Shared project configs. Teams get the vetted servers through a checked-in .mcp.json, so every developer's agent sees the same tool surface on day one.
  3. Per-user, least-privilege auth. Remote MCP servers authenticate with OAuth 2.0, so each developer signs in as themselves with narrowly scoped permissions (read-only issue tracker, for example), instead of sharing one static API key baked into a file. When someone leaves, you revoke their grant; nobody else is affected.

There is a deeper reason architects care. Every MCP server you add expands three things at once: the agent's capabilities (what it can do), the attack surface (what a compromised or malicious server can do), and the token cost (tool definitions consume context on every request). This is the D3 "capability bloat" idea applied to developer tooling: the tool list is an architecture decision, not plumbing.

Worked example (illustrative). A 60-person org vets three MCP servers: docs search (read-only), issue tracker (read-only), and CI status (read-only). A team requests a fourth: a database admin server with write access, "to speed up debugging." Registry review rejects write access and approves a read-only variant. Two months later that server's upstream dependency is compromised; because access was read-only and per-user OAuth, the blast radius is contained to reads, and the security team revokes the server from the registry in one place instead of hunting through 60 personal configs.

Common misunderstanding

"MCP config is just developer convenience." On this exam, the MCP tool list is a security and cost surface. A scenario that mentions unvetted servers, shared static keys, or "agents can suddenly do more than expected" is testing whether you centralize distribution with scoped auth, not whether developers find the config convenient.

Exam relevance: D7 tests the distribution mechanism against a constraint. "Revocable centrally" or "contractor leaves" points to per-user OAuth via a managed registry. "Consistent tool surface" points to checked-in project .mcp.json.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A team shares a .mcp.json containing a database MCP server configured with a single shared API key committed in the file. A contractor with repo access leaves the company." Select two.

Trap: "rotate the shared key immediately" is only half the fix; it treats the symptom. The credited pair identifies the design flaw (shared static credential with no per-user identity, committed in version control) and the structural fix (per-user OAuth with least-privilege scopes, secrets in a vault, server vetted through the registry). Rotating the key without changing the pattern guarantees a repeat.

4. AI-assisted development workflows: where AI helps, where humans gate

What it is. AI-assisted development means AI tools participate in the normal dev loop: drafting code, generating tests, explaining legacy code, refactoring, writing docs. The architect's job is not to "allow AI" or "ban AI." It is to design the workflow: which tasks the AI may do freely, and which gates every AI-produced change must pass before it ships.

Why it exists. AI output is fluent and confident, which makes its failure modes sneaky: hallucinated APIs that look real, insecure patterns (string-concatenated SQL), outdated library usage, subtly wrong business logic. Without gates, you do not get faster engineering; you get defects at machine speed. The workflow is what converts raw generation into reliable throughput.

Under the hood: draft with AI, verify with determinism

The pattern that works is a split of responsibilities. The AI drafts; deterministic systems and humans verify. Concretely:

  • Green tier (AI-friendly): boilerplate, test scaffolding from a spec, docstrings, explaining unfamiliar code, small refactors with full test coverage. Light review.
  • Yellow tier (review carefully): new business logic, refactors touching shared code, dependency changes. The reviewer reads for behavior, not style: does it do the right thing at the boundaries?
  • Red tier (senior gate): authentication, cryptography, database migrations, anything irreversible or security-sensitive. Requires senior review and passing tests, no exceptions.

Verification is layered: compiler and type checker catch syntax and type errors; linters catch style and known-bad patterns; the test suite catches behavior regressions; the human reviewer catches wrong requirements and wrong assumptions. No single layer is enough, because each catches a different class of mistake.

Worked example (illustrative). A team measures its first quarter with AI assistance: PRs merge about 30% faster, but PRs with no test changes show roughly double the revert rate of PRs with tests. The team responds with a workflow rule, not a ban: every AI-generated change must either include tests or carry an explicit reviewer sign-off noting why tests were skipped. Revert rates converge back to baseline within a quarter, and velocity stays up.

Common misunderstanding

"The AI wrote tests, so the change is tested." Generated tests can encode the same misunderstanding as the generated code: if the AI misread the requirement, its tests will assert the wrong behavior and pass. Tests are only as good as the specification they encode. On review, the question is never "are there tests" but "do the tests assert the specified behavior, and who verified the spec?"

Exam relevance: D7 asks you to design the workflow under a constraint. Regulated industry or security-sensitive code points to mandatory human gates at the red tier. Velocity complaints point to keeping green-tier friction near zero, not to removing gates.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "After adopting AI coding tools, a team's PR velocity doubles but production incidents rise. Investigation shows AI-generated PRs are being rubber-stamped. Which two changes best address this?" Select two.

Trap: "ban AI tools for production code" (throws away the velocity) or "require longer review checklists" (checklists get skimmed). The credited pair targets the failure mode: tiered review gates (red-tier changes need senior review plus tests) and behavior-level review standards (reviewers verify what the code does at boundaries, and generated tests are checked against the spec, not just executed).

5. Secrets and data governance in AI tooling

What it is. Secrets and data governance answers one question: what information is allowed to flow into AI tools, and what must never leave the org's boundary? Secrets are credentials (API keys, passwords, private keys, tokens). Data governance covers the rest: customer PII (personally identifiable information), source code from restricted repos, internal documents. A prompt is data, and data sent to a tool can end up in logs, vendor systems, or training pipelines depending on the provider's policy.

Why it exists. Developers paste secrets into AI tools for the most sympathetic reason: they are debugging, and the secret is part of the broken context. One pasted production key is a full incident: rotate the credential, audit for misuse, explain it to security. Prevention is orders of magnitude cheaper than the incident.

Under the hood: four layers of defense

  1. Policy: a written rule for what data classes may go to which tools. For example: public code may go anywhere; internal code only to tools under the org's data agreement; customer PII and secrets to no AI tool at all. Where available, use zero-data-retention (ZDR) terms so the vendor does not retain prompts.
  2. Prevention: make the mistake hard to commit. A PreToolUse hook scans prompts and tool inputs for secret patterns (sk-..., AKIA..., PEM private-key headers) and blocks the call before the model sees anything. Developers reference secrets by name ("use the DB_PASSWORD env var"), never by value. Sensitive paths are excluded from what the agent may read, like a .gitignore for the agent's eyes.
  3. Detection: stored transcripts and logs are redacted (secret-shaped strings replaced before writing), and secret scanning runs over repos and logs to catch what slipped through.
  4. Response: a rotation runbook: which credential, who owns it, how fast it can be replaced, who gets notified.

Worked example (illustrative). An org deploys the secret-scanning hook to all 200 developers. In the first month it blocks 34 paste attempts, most of them AWS-style keys pasted during debugging sessions. Each block shows the developer a message: "Blocked: this looks like a credential. Reference it by environment variable name instead." Paste attempts drop by 80% in the second month, because the hook is also a teacher.

Common misunderstanding

"We have an enterprise agreement with zero data retention, so pasting secrets is fine." Two holes. First, ZDR covers the vendor's API, not your laptop: local transcripts, shell history, and your own logs may still hold the secret. Second, retention terms are about storage, not about the human and system exposure in between. The rule stands regardless of contract: reference secrets by name, never by value, and a leaked credential gets rotated even if you believe nobody retained it.

Exam relevance: D7 tests prevention over detection. When the scenario describes a leak vector, the credited control is the one that stops the data from leaving the boundary (hook, reference-by-name), not the one that finds it afterward (scanning, audit).

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An engineer pastes a production database password into Claude Code while debugging a connection issue. The org's vendor agreement includes zero data retention." Select two.

Trap: "no action needed, ZDR means the vendor retained nothing." The credited pair: rotate the credential immediately (local transcripts, shell history, and logs are outside ZDR's scope) and add a PreToolUse hook that blocks secret-shaped input before it reaches the model, so the next tired engineer cannot repeat it.

6. Debugging production Claude systems: trace forensics

What it is. Debugging a production Claude system means figuring out why the agent did the wrong thing: the wrong tool, the wrong arguments, a loop, a confident but false answer. Because you cannot attach a debugger to a conversation, you debug with traces: the complete record of a request. A trace holds the system prompt, every message, every tool_use block with its exact input, every tool_result, the stop_reason of each step (why the model stopped: tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens), token counts, latencies, and a correlation ID tying it all to one user session.

Why it exists. LLM failures are non-deterministic and stateful: the same prompt can produce different behavior on different runs, and each step depends on everything before it. Without traces you are left with "it worked when I tried it," which resolves nothing. The trace is the core dump of an agentic system.

Under the hood: the forensics workflow

  1. Capture everything, keyed by correlation ID. Log the full request/response cycle: model version, temperature, system prompt, tool schemas, every tool input and result. The correlation ID must flow through your stack so one user complaint maps to one trace.
  2. Read the stop reasons first. max_tokens means "the model was cut off mid-thought," which is a budget problem, not a reasoning problem. tool_use versus end_turn tells you whether the model chose to act or chose to answer.
  3. Inspect the tool_use / tool_result pairs. Most production bugs live here: the model passed the wrong argument, or the tool returned something unexpected and the model coped badly. Check the tool schemas too: if a schema changed (a field renamed, a type changed from string to number) the model may be calling a contract that no longer exists. Schema drift is a classic.
  4. Reproduce with frozen inputs. Re-running the prompt is not reproduction: temperature above zero and live tool results make every run diverge. True reproduction means replaying the trace with identical inputs: same model version, same system prompt, and canned tool results recorded from the failing run. If the replay diverges, the nondeterminism itself is a clue.
  5. Binary-search the trace. Replay up to tool call N with canned results and see where behavior first goes wrong. The fault is between the last good step and the first bad one.

Worked example (illustrative). Support ticket: "the assistant booked the wrong hotel dates." The trace (14 tool calls, ~38k input tokens) shows the fault at call 9: the hotel search tool returned dates in DD/MM/YYYY after a vendor update, but the agent's instructions assumed MM/DD/YYYY. The model did not misbehave; it faithfully used a mislabeled input. Fix: normalize dates in the tool wrapper (deterministic code), not a prompt tweak. The forensics took 20 minutes because the trace was complete; without it, the team would have spent days prompt-tuning a data bug.

Common misunderstanding

"Re-running the prompt reproduces the bug." It does not, unless you freeze everything the run depended on. Temperature, model version, the system prompt, the tool schemas, and every tool result are all inputs. Change any of them and you are debugging a different incident. Frozen replay with canned tool results is the bar for "reproduced."

Exam relevance: D7's "support debugging" objective is diagnostic reasoning. Given a symptom, the credited move is the artifact that localizes the fault fastest: stop reasons for cut-off behavior, tool_use/tool_result pairs for wrong actions, schema history for intermittent wrong-tool calls.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An agent intermittently calls the wrong tool. The prompts in the failing traces are identical to the prompts in successful traces." Select one.

Trap: "lower the temperature" or "rewrite the system prompt." Identical prompts producing different behavior means the non-prompt inputs changed. The credited answer checks the tool definitions and their recent change history (schema drift: a renamed field, a changed description, a newly added overlapping tool) and the contents of the tool results, before touching the prompt at all.

7. Operational runbooks for LLM apps

What it is. A runbook is the written procedure the on-call engineer follows when something breaks: symptoms, what to check, what to do, in what order. LLM apps need runbooks for failure modes traditional runbooks never imagined: runaway agentic loops (the agent calls tools forever), cost spikes (a loop burning money), prompt-injection attempts, context-window overflow (the conversation outgrows the model's memory), and behavior drift after a model version change.

Why it exists. At 3am nobody reasons from first principles. The runbook converts judgment into a checklist, so the response is fast and consistent no matter who is on call. It also encodes the lesson of every previous incident, so the org only pays for each failure mode once.

Under the hood: the incident loop

Every LLM runbook page follows the same four phases:

  1. Detect. Alerts on leading indicators, not just outages: tool calls per session, tokens per session, spend per hour, error rate on tool calls, injection-pattern matches. If you only alert on "the app is down," a cost spike can burn money for hours while the app looks healthy.
  2. Triage. Scope the blast radius: how many sessions, which users, since when, which model version and prompt version. Grab the correlation IDs; you will need the traces later.
  3. Mitigate. Stop the bleeding before diagnosing. The kill switches: disable the agent endpoint, revoke the API key, flip the feature flag, cap max tool iterations per session, enforce a per-session spend limit. Mitigation buys time; it is not the fix.
  4. Root cause and harden. Now do the trace forensics from Section 6. Every incident must end with a hardening item: a guardrail, a cap, a validation, or a test that makes this class of incident impossible or self-limiting. An incident with no hardening item will recur.

The guardrails that make runbooks work are built before the incident: per-request timeouts, max iterations per agent session, spend alerts with automatic caps, circuit breakers on failing tools. A runbook without these is a checklist with no levers.

IncidentLeading signalFirst action (mitigate)Hardening
Runaway agentic loopTool calls/session far above baselineKill the sessions, cap max iterationsIdempotent tools, max-retry in wrappers
Cost spikeSpend/hour alertPer-session spend cap, disable endpoint if neededBudget alerts with auto-throttle
Prompt injection attemptInjection-pattern match in inputsBlock the session, preserve the traceInput validation, least-privilege tools
Context overflowToken counts near the limit, truncated outputsFail gracefully with a summary promptCompaction strategy, shorter tool results
Behavior drift (new model version)Eval scores or task success drop after deployRoll back to the pinned versionPin versions, eval gate on every upgrade

Worked example (illustrative). At 2am the spend dashboard spikes to 40x baseline. Alert: sessions averaging 300+ tool calls. On-call follows the runbook: kills the affected sessions via the admin API and flips on the 25-iteration cap (mitigation, 8 minutes). Traces show a tool that always returned "retry," which the agent obeyed forever. Root cause fixed the next day: the tool wrapper now returns a terminal error after 3 retries. Hardening: the iteration cap and a per-session spend limit of $5 stay on permanently. Total burn: about $180 over 20 minutes. Without the runbook's kill switch, the loop would have run until morning standup.

Common misunderstanding

"The runbook is the fix." The runbook is time-buying. Mitigation stops the damage; the fix is the code change; the prevention is the hardening item. Teams that stop at mitigation collect the same incident every quarter. The exam will offer "follow the runbook's mitigation steps" as a distractor when the question asks for the lasting fix, and vice versa.

Exam relevance: D7's "operational issue resolution" maps directly to this loop. The exam rewards mitigate-before-diagnose ordering and kill-switch selection matched to the failure mode.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "At 2am the spend dashboard spikes 40x. Agent sessions show 300+ tool calls each. Two candidate first actions: (a) read the traces to find the bug, (b) kill the sessions and enforce an iteration cap, then investigate." Select one, with justification.

Trap: (a) feels diligent: the engineer wants to understand before acting. But every minute of diagnosis is money burning and the loop is still running. The credited answer is (b): stop the bleed first, then diagnose. A follow-up item will then ask for the hardening change (iteration caps, idempotent tools, spend limits), which is where the lasting fix lives.

Exam-day notes for D7

How to spend your study time on the smallest domain

  • Four questions, scenario-shaped. D7 is 7% of the exam, roughly 4 of 63 items. Each one is a production scenario with a constraint. Do not memorize config file paths; practice constraint-first reading: find the constraint in the scenario ("even if a developer edits local files," "must never," "at 2am"), then pick the control that satisfies it.
  • "Most correct" distractors are the norm. Several options will be partially right. Ask which option guarantees the outcome under the stated constraint: deny beats ask, prevention beats detection, mitigation beats diagnosis, managed layer beats project settings.
  • Know the order of operations. Rollout: managed policy first, then project conventions, then personal settings. Incident: detect, triage, mitigate, root-cause, harden. Debug: correlation ID, stop reasons, tool pairs, frozen replay. If an answer choice violates the order, it is wrong.
  • Watch for the human-weakness traps. "Ask the developer to approve" fails under deadline pressure. "Review the prompt" fails when inputs changed. "Rely on the vendor agreement" fails for local data. The exam keeps testing whether you design for how systems actually fail, not how they should behave.
You might be wondering: do I need hands-on Claude Code experience for these questions?

It helps, but the questions are pitched at the architect level: rollout design, policy layering, workflow gates, incident response. If you understand the four configuration layers, the allow/ask/deny trade-off, the draft-and-gate workflow, frozen-replay debugging, and the mitigate-before-diagnose runbook loop, you can answer every D7 scenario from this volume alone. The exam explicitly tests design decisions and trade-offs, not config trivia.
